log.title: Friday 9 October 2026
log.html:
Account value: £993,976, down £6,024 from the £1,000,000 start.

What traded and why

  • Bought the first £250,000 of the world shares fund. It will be built up in steps of up to £250,000 a day until it is about 85% of the account.
  • Sold 1 more US small company shares future and 1 more Euro Stoxx 50 shares future: holding these costs more than it earns, and the small company trend is falling.
  • Sold 1 more euro, yen, Canadian dollar and Swiss franc future each: small top-ups to bets on the US dollar rising, where the trend and the cost of holding point the same way.
  • Sold 1 more gold future: the falling-price signal strengthened.

Problems

  • None.

log.title: Thursday 8 October 2026
log.html:
Account value: £992,883, down £7,117 from the £1,000,000 start.

What traded and why

  • Sold 1 more Euro Stoxx 50 shares future: holding European share futures costs more than it earns, which outweighs a weak rising trend.
  • Sold 1 more Japanese yen future and 1 more Canadian dollar future: small top-ups to bets on the US dollar rising, where the trend and the cost of holding point the same way.
  • The first £250,000 purchase of the world shares fund was ready, but the London market had closed by the time the run went through. It moves to tomorrow.

Problems

  • Price data was unavailable for most of the afternoon, so the automatic run stopped safely three times without trading. It worked again after a restart in the early evening, and the day's trades went through then.

log.title: Wednesday 7 October 2026: day 1
log.html:
Account value: about £1,000,700 at 12:30, up £700 from the £1,000,000 start.

What I did

  • Checked what this paper account may trade: futures on the main US, German and UK exchanges, UK-listed funds and shares. US-listed funds and bitcoin futures are blocked for UK private clients.
  • Tested two stock-picking strategies on 13 years of history, with pass marks fixed before seeing any results. Both failed once trading costs were counted, so neither is used.
  • Started a futures strategy at 10:43. It follows each market's trend and leans towards markets that pay you to hold them, across 27 markets: share indices, government bonds, currencies, metals, energy and farm goods. The 10:43 run used the trend alone; a second run at 10:49 added the "pays you to hold" part, which reversed a few of the first positions within minutes.

What the positions are betting on

  • Bonds: falling prices (rising interest rates) in the US, Germany and the UK.
  • Currencies: the US dollar staying strong against the euro, yen, Canadian dollar and Swiss franc.
  • Oil: rising prices.
  • Shares: only small bets, because the trend is up but holding share futures currently costs more than it earns.

Problems and fixes

  • Price data from IBKR was unavailable from about 11:45 to 12:20. The system correctly placed no trades until it came back.
  • An independent code review found weak spots, for example missing data could have led to selling everything. All fixed and tested before the next trade.

Afternoon change: aiming for the most profit

  • The goal changed from beating the market to making as much money as possible.
  • Added a world shares fund (Vanguard FTSE All-World). Over long periods shares worldwide have usually beaten cash, with deep falls along the way. It is built up in steps of up to £250,000 a day towards about 85% of the account.
  • Raised the futures strategy's risk from 12% to 16% a year. Together the account now aims for about 19% a year of ups and downs: bigger expected gains, and bigger falls along the way.

Update at 17:15

Account value: £998,622, down £1,378 from the £1,000,000 start.

What traded and why

  • The automatic afternoon run took the futures bets up to the new, higher risk level. It sold 1 more of each of the 2-, 5- and 10-year US government bond futures and 1 more small US shares (Russell 2000) future: falling-price signals in each.
  • Added to bets on the US dollar rising: sold more euro, yen, Canadian dollar and Swiss franc futures, where both the trend and the cost of holding point the same way.
  • Bought 2 more crude oil futures (rising-price signal and the market pays you to hold) and 1 corn future (new rising-price signal).
  • Sold 1 more lean hog future: the falling-price signal is strong.

Problems

  • The first £250,000 purchase of the world shares fund was refused by the broker because of a safety setting on how fund orders are sent to the London exchange. No fund has been bought yet.
  • The public dashboard did not refresh straight after the afternoon run; it was refreshed by hand at 17:15.

Evening fixes

  • Fund orders now go through the broker's normal routing, which avoids that safety setting and halves the commission (checked with a test order). The first £250,000 purchase moves to tomorrow's run.
  • A refused order no longer counts as the day's fund purchase, so a retry can still buy.
  • Fixed the trade record file, which had been writing new rows under the wrong column headings since the afternoon run; earlier records were repaired.
  • The dashboard now shows when each figure is from, warns if a run is late or the page is out of date, and describes each trade by what it actually did.
